title: "Data"
subtitle: "Loading, joining, cleaning, and validating the Olist dataset"
---

## Overview and Analytical Goal
 To predict order delivery duration (`delivery_days`), I first assemble a single, analysis ready dataset. In this page, I load the six source tables, verify table dimensions and keys, merge them at the order item level, document every cleaning and missing data rule with row counts, run baseline sanity checks, and save the cleaned dataset for exploration in further steps.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)
```

## Step 1: Loading the Six Raw Olist Tables
 Read the six raw CSV files (customers, category_translation, order_items, orders, products, and sellers)

```{r}
customers <- read_csv("data/customers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
category_translation <- read_csv("data/category_translation.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

raw_table_summary <- tibble(
  table_name = c("order_items", "orders", "customers", "products", "sellers", "category_translation"),
  rows = c(nrow(order_items), nrow(orders), nrow(customers), nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(category_translation)),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(orders), ncol(customers), ncol(products), ncol(sellers), ncol(category_translation)),
  primary_key = c("order_id + order_item_id", "order_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "seller_id", "product_category_name")
)

kable(
  raw_table_summary,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Table Name", "Row Count", "Column Count", "Join / Primary Key"),
  caption = "Dimensions and join keys of the six raw Olist tables"
)
```

 order_items `r format(nrow(order_items), big.mark = ",") rows` is more granular than orders `r format(nrow(orders), big.mark = ","` rows) because a single order can contain multiple items or sellers.

One row is one order at Olist website : one order, its customer, its order status, and its delivery days. The file holds `r nrow(orders)` rows and `r ncol(orders)` columns, covering `r n_distinct(orders$order_id)` orders and `r n_distinct(orders$customer_id)` customers.

```{r}
glimpse(customers)
glimpse(category_translation)
glimpse(order_items)
glimpse(orders)
glimpse(products)
glimpse(sellers)
```

## Data dictionary
Customers Table
| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
customer_id	text	Id per order, links orders to customers
customer_unique_id	text	Permanent id of a real customer
customer_zip_code_prefix	number	First 5 digits of zip code
customer_city	text	Customer’s city
customer_state	text	Two-letter state code

Order_items Table
| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
order_id	text	Id of the order
order_item_id	integer	Item position within the order
product_id	text	Id of the product
seller_id	text	Id of the seller
shipping_limit_date	datetime	Seller’s deadline to ship the item
price	number	Item price in BRL
freight_value	number	Shipping cost in BRL

Category_translation Table
| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
product_category_name	text	Category name in Portuguese
product_category_name_english	text	Category name in English


Orders Table
| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
order_id	text	Id of the order
order_item_id	integer	Item position in the order
product_id	text	Id of the product
seller_id	text	Id of the seller
shipping_limit_date	datetime	Seller’s shipping deadline
price	number	Item price in BRL
freight_value	number	Shipping cost 


Products Table
| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
product_id	text	Id of the product
product_category_name	text	Product category in Portuguese
product_name_lenght	number	Characters in the product name
product_description_lenght	number	Characters in the product description
product_photos_qty	number	Number of published photos
product_weight_g	number	Weight in grams
product_length_cm	number	Length in cm
product_height_cm	number	Height in cm
product_width_cm	number	Width in cm

sellers Table
| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
seller_id	text	Id of the seller
seller_zip_code_prefix	number	First 5 digits of zip code
seller_city	text	Seller’s city
seller_state	text	Two-letter state code

## Step 2: Joining the Six Tables into One Master Dataset
 What this step does: Uses order_items as the base table and performs five sequential left_join() operations (orders, customers, products, category_translation, and sellers) so every item retains its order timestamps, buyer/seller locations, and physical product specs. I compared row counts before and after joining to ensure no accidental many-to-many row duplication occurred.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
rows_before_join <- nrow(order_items)

df_master <- order_items |>
  left_join(orders, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(customers, by = "customer_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  left_join(category_translation, by = "product_category_name") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id")

rows_after_join <- nrow(df_master)

join_check <- tibble(
  stage = c("Before joins (order_items)", "After joining all 6 tables (df_master)"),
  rows = c(rows_before_join, rows_after_join),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(df_master))
)

kable(
  join_check,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Pipeline Stage", "Row Count", "Column Count"),
  caption = "Row-count validation before and after merging the six Olist tables"
)
```
 The row count stays identical at r format `(rows_after_join, big.mark = ",") rows` across `r ncol(df_master)` columns, confirming a clean one-to-one lookup match across all six tables with zero row inflation


### Step 3: Auditing Missing Values and Cleaning Rules
 What this step does: First audits missing values across every column in the joined dataset, then applies four targeted cleaning rules: fixing misspelled column names, standardizing monthly purchase dates, removing rows where the target (delivery_days) is missing, and imputing missing product metadata.

```{r}
na_before <- tibble(
  column = names(df_master),
  missing_count = colSums(is.na(df_master)),
  missing_pct = round(100 * colSums(is.na(df_master)) / nrow(df_master), 2)
) |>
  filter(missing_count > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_count))

kable(
  na_before,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Column Name", "Missing Rows", "Missing Share (%)"),
  caption = "Columns with missing values in the raw joined dataset"
)
```

```{r}
rows_initial <- nrow(df_master)
missing_del_n <- sum(is.na(df_master$delivery_days))

df_master <- df_master |>
  rename(
    product_name_length = product_name_lenght,
    product_description_length = product_description_lenght
  ) |>
  mutate(
    purchase_year_month = make_date(purchase_year, purchase_month, 1)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))

rows_after_target_filter <- nrow(df_master)

df_master <- df_master |>
  mutate(
    product_category_name = if_else(is.na(product_category_name), "unknown", product_category_name),
    product_category_name_english = if_else(
      is.na(product_category_name_english),
      product_category_name,
      product_category_name_english
    ),
    across(
      c(
        product_name_length,
        product_description_length,
        product_photos_qty,
        product_weight_g,
        product_length_cm,
        product_height_cm,
        product_width_cm
      ),
      ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)
    )
  )
```

 After applying these rules, `r sum(colSums(is.na(df_master)))` missing values remain across all `r ncol(df_master)` columns in `r format(nrow(df_master), big.mark = ",")` rows `(r format(n_distinct(df_master$order_id), big.mark = ",")` unique orders)


### Step 4: Baseline Sanity Checks (Status, Target Summary, Timing, and Geography)
 What this step does: Verifies that order statuses, target summary metrics, purchase dates, and seller states behave sensibly before moving to exploratory visualization.

## Order Status and Cancellation Rate


```{r}
status_summary <- df_master |>
  count(order_status, name = "order_item_rows") |>
  mutate(
    pct_rows = round(100 * order_item_rows / sum(order_item_rows), 4)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(order_item_rows))

kable(
  status_summary,
  digits = 4,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Order Status", "Order-Item Rows", "Share (%)"),
  caption = "Order-item rows and percentage share by order status"
)
```
Nearly all rows with an observed `delivery_days` value are `"delivered"`, while `"canceled"` orders account for only `r status_summary$order_item_rows[status_summary$order_status == "canceled"]` rows `(r status_summary$pct_rows[status_summary$order_status == "canceled"]% cancellation rate)`, showing negligible cancellation noise in the target dataset.

## Overall delivery_days Summary

```{r}
overall_del_summary <- df_master |>
  summarise(
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id)
  )

kable(
  overall_del_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Min Days", "Mean Days", "Median Days", "Max Days", "SD Days", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Baseline summary statistics for delivery_days across cleaned orders"
)
```

Across `r format(overall_del_summary$num_orders, big.mark = ",")` orders, `delivery_days` averages `r round(overall_del_summary$avg_days, 2)` days compared with a median of `r round(overall_del_summary$median_days, 2)` days and a maximum of `r round(overall_del_summary$max_days, 1)` days, indicating a right-skewed tail of slow deliveries.


## Order Volume and Delivery Time by Day of Week and Purchase Span

```{r}
weekday_summary <- df_master |>
  group_by(purchase_day_of_week) |>
  summarise(
    avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(num_orders))

kable(
  weekday_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Purchase Day", "Mean Days", "Max Days", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Order volume and delivery duration by purchase day of week"
)

date_range_summary <- df_master |>
  summarise(
    min_month = min(purchase_year_month),
    max_month = max(purchase_year_month),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id)
  )

kable(
  date_range_summary,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Earliest Month", "Latest Month", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Purchase date coverage in the cleaned dataset"
)
```
The dataset covers `r date_range_summary$min_month` through `r date_range_summary$max_month`, with order volume peaking on weekdays and average `delivery_days` remaining relatively stable across days of the week.



## Delivery Performance by Seller State

```{r}
seller_state_summary <- df_master |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_days))

kable(
  seller_state_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Seller State", "Mean Days", "Median Days", "Min Days", "Max Days", "SD Days", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Delivery days and order volume by seller state (full width)"
)
```

Seller activity is heavily concentrated in `SP` `(r format(seller_state_summary$num_orders[seller_state_summary$seller_state == "SP"], big.mark = ",")` orders), whereas remote states like `AM` show much higher mean delivery times `(r round(seller_state_summary$avg_days[seller_state_summary$seller_state == "AM"], 1)` days) on very small order counts `(r seller_state_summary$num_orders[seller_state_summary$seller_state == "AM"]` orders).

## Step 5: Saving the Cleaned Dataset and Next Step
 With df_master_clean.rds verified and saved, the Exploration page examines the distribution of delivery_days first, then tests how delivery duration varies across geography, purchase month, shipping cost, and product weight/categories

```{r}

#| include: false
write_rds(df_master, "data/df_master_clean.rds")

```
